newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia says timber costs up 75 percent.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia says timber costs up 75 percent.

text.p: The British Columbia government released an analysis of the forest industry on Friday that showed timber costs have risen 75 percent since 1992.
The study by consultants KPMG found the cost of a delivered cubic metre of wood rose to C$86.74 in 1996 from C$49.57 in 1992. It looked at 94 forest operations.

The report said that the C$37.17 cost increase consisted of C$12.22 in costs related to meeting the government's new forest practices code, C$16.55 to increased stumpage fees and royalty paymenbts and C$8.40 to other factors.
The report was likely to intensify complaints from the forest industry.

The government has faced harsh criticism from forest companies like MacMillan Bloedel Ltd who contend that more onerous regulations and higher government-imposed costs threaten the industry's viability in British Columbia.

A group of about 20 forest company presidents and government officials have been negotiating for weeks on a jobs and timber accord. This would seek to increase employment in the forest sector by 20,000 jobs by 2000 in exchange for easing of bureaucracy and costs.

But Premier Glen Clark has ruled out any major reduction in stumpage costs and provincial officials have said that any changes are likely to be incremental, rather than the wholesale revamp that the industry has sought.
Forests Minister David Zirnhelt said Friday that the cost analysis would be used by the government to ensure its policies were "effective and efficient."
"The government is not prepared to weaken our world-leading standards for forests practices," he said.

"However, there may be opportunities to cut red tape and eliminate administrative duplication which could have a positive impact on the forest sector's ability to continue its substantial contributions to the B.C. economy."
While noting that costs have risen, he said forest industry revenues have risen 45 percent during the period and lumber prices have risen 58 percent.
